questions.prompt: A portable imaging unit enters the OR. What protects personnel during exposure?
options: Use the planned shielding, distance, and exposure communication process.
Cluster staff next to the beam.
Remove protective garments for mobility.
Assume shielding is unnecessary for brief images.
questions.explanation: Radiation protection depends on positioning and communication at each exposure.
whyOthers: That choice does not address the central safety requirement. Radiation protection depends on positioning and communication at each exposure.
Removing it in this way loses a needed barrier, record, or control. Radiation protection depends on positioning and communication at each exposure.
The assumption is unverified and could miss the relevant risk. Radiation protection depends on positioning and communication at each exposure.

questions.prompt: A critical monitor displays implausible values. What should the team do?
options: Assess the patient and verify the equipment before relying on the reading.
Treat the number as correct without assessment.
Disable all monitoring for the rest of the case.
Ask the device vendor to decide treatment alone.
questions.explanation: Patient assessment and equipment troubleshooting proceed together.
whyOthers: That applies the wrong classification or care process. Patient assessment and equipment troubleshooting proceed together.
That choice does not address the central safety requirement. Patient assessment and equipment troubleshooting proceed together.
That person or step cannot replace the responsible clinical process. Patient assessment and equipment troubleshooting proceed together.

questions.prompt: A specimen's laterality does not match the label prepared in advance. What should the nurse do?
options: Pause and verify the site and patient details with the team before the specimen leaves the OR.
Send it and correct the label later.
Use the schedule side without asking.
Combine it with another specimen.
questions.explanation: Specimen labeling must reflect the actual collection site and patient.
whyOthers: Sending it before verification or safe handling can propagate an error. Specimen labeling must reflect the actual collection site and patient.
The proposed substitute does not establish the required safe process. Specimen labeling must reflect the actual collection site and patient.
That choice does not address the central safety requirement. Specimen labeling must reflect the actual collection site and patient.

questions.prompt: A patient receiving moderate sedation becomes less responsive. What must continue?
options: Continuous assessment and readiness to support airway, ventilation, and circulation.
Only a pulse check at discharge.
Only observation of the surgical site.
Monitoring only if the patient complains.
questions.explanation: Sedation depth may change and demands ongoing physiological assessment.
whyOthers: Focusing on just one detail omits other needed checks or controls. Sedation depth may change and demands ongoing physiological assessment.
Focusing on just one detail omits other needed checks or controls. Sedation depth may change and demands ongoing physiological assessment.
That single measure leaves other necessary controls unaddressed. Sedation depth may change and demands ongoing physiological assessment.

questions.prompt: A patient is exposed to plume during surgery. Why is evacuation also relevant to the patient?
options: Source control reduces particulate and chemical exposure within the operative environment.
Only staff can be exposed.
A drape makes the plume harmless.
Plume is identical to sterile steam.
questions.explanation: Plume is a shared patient and worker safety concern.
whyOthers: Focusing on just one detail omits other needed checks or controls. Plume is a shared patient and worker safety concern.
That choice does not address the central safety requirement. Plume is a shared patient and worker safety concern.
That choice does not address the central safety requirement. Plume is a shared patient and worker safety concern.

questions.prompt: A new device needs single-use accessories. What should procurement plan?
options: Reliable compatible supply, cost, storage, and disposal before adoption.
Only the capital purchase.
An unapproved substitute if stock runs out.
No storage space because accessories are small.
questions.explanation: Equipment availability depends on its ongoing consumables and support.
whyOthers: Focusing on just one detail omits other needed checks or controls. Equipment availability depends on its ongoing consumables and support.
An unverified or unauthorized approach cannot establish safe care. Equipment availability depends on its ongoing consumables and support.
That choice does not address the central safety requirement. Equipment availability depends on its ongoing consumables and support.

questions.prompt: A maintenance check finds a fault in an otherwise needed device. What is the safe resource decision?
options: Remove or restrict the device and arrange repair and a checked alternative.
Ignore the fault during busy days.
Change the maintenance record to passed.
Move the device to another OR without warning.
questions.explanation: Maintenance findings must lead to usable, safe equipment decisions.
whyOthers: Ignoring the finding leaves the possible problem unassessed. Maintenance findings must lead to usable, safe equipment decisions.
Changing a record or setting without verification hides the actual issue. Maintenance findings must lead to usable, safe equipment decisions.
Moving it this way bypasses separation or verification controls. Maintenance findings must lead to usable, safe equipment decisions.

questions.prompt: What does a perioperative nursing mission contribute to day-to-day decisions?
options: A shared purpose for safe, evidence-informed, patient-centred practice.
A substitute for assessing each patient.
Permission to disregard regulation.
A guarantee that every outcome is identical.
questions.explanation: A mission frames why the specialty organizes and improves perioperative care.
whyOthers: That choice does not address the central safety requirement. A mission frames why the specialty organizes and improves perioperative care.
That choice does not address the central safety requirement. A mission frames why the specialty organizes and improves perioperative care.
That choice does not address the central safety requirement. A mission frames why the specialty organizes and improves perioperative care.

questions.prompt: A team discusses the future direction of perioperative nursing. Which foundation is most relevant?
options: A vision that guides improvement and collaboration across practice settings.
Only the next day's surgical schedule.
A list of individual equipment preferences.
A fixed plan that excludes new evidence.
questions.explanation: A vision describes the desired direction of professional practice.
whyOthers: Focusing on just one detail omits other needed checks or controls. A vision describes the desired direction of professional practice.
That choice does not address the central safety requirement. A vision describes the desired direction of professional practice.
That choice does not address the central safety requirement. A vision describes the desired direction of professional practice.

questions.prompt: Before the first case, what preliminary cleaning step should be considered?
options: Inspect the room and damp-dust horizontal surfaces with the approved product before supplies arrive.
Bring in sterile supplies before checking surfaces.
Use a dry feather duster over the field.
Wait for end-of-day cleaning to remove dust.
questions.explanation: Preliminary cleaning addresses accumulated dust before sterile setup and patient entry.
whyOthers: That choice does not address the central safety requirement. Preliminary cleaning addresses accumulated dust before sterile setup and patient entry.
The proposed substitute does not establish the required safe process. Preliminary cleaning addresses accumulated dust before sterile setup and patient entry.
Waiting delays a step that is needed before the risk develops. Preliminary cleaning addresses accumulated dust before sterile setup and patient entry.

questions.prompt: A nurse is authorized by law to perform a task but lacks current competence. What else must be established?
options: The knowledge, skills, and judgment to perform it safely within the organizational role.
Legal scope alone proves readiness.
An informal request replaces training.
Competence matters only after an incident.
questions.explanation: Scope, role, practice guidance, and individual competence are distinct decision factors.
whyOthers: That single measure leaves other necessary controls unaddressed. Scope, role, practice guidance, and individual competence are distinct decision factors.
That choice does not address the central safety requirement. Scope, role, practice guidance, and individual competence are distinct decision factors.

cases.CASE01: An adult is scheduled for a left knee procedure. During preparation, the team checks the record, consent, site mark, and planned time-out.
cases.CASE02: An adult is preparing for major abdominal surgery. The team reviews allergies, infection prevention, temperature management, and clot risk.
cases.CASE03: An anesthetized patient is transferred and positioned for a prolonged prone procedure. Skin, pressure, nerve, and handoff risks are considered.
cases.CASE04: During an open abdominal procedure, sponges are used and the closing count does not reconcile. The team must prevent an unintentionally retained item.
cases.CASE05: During surgery, a verbal order is given and specimens are sent for time-sensitive analysis. Several clear solutions are on the field.
cases.CASE06: Before anesthesia, a family history raises concern for malignant hyperthermia. The team reviews preparedness and recognition of a possible crisis.
cases.CASE07: A robotic minimally invasive operation is planned with some staff new to the platform. The team reviews docking, emergency access, and plume controls.
cases.CASE08: An urgent operation is needed for a patient with suspected respiratory infection. Airway management and subsequent room turnover require planning.
cases.CASE09: A joint replacement is scheduled. A loaned tray and implant arrive, and the team assesses validated processing and load release before use.
cases.CASE10: A head and neck procedure uses oxygen and surgical energy after skin preparation. The team is concerned about fire prevention and safe electrode handling.
cases.CASE11: An extremity operation requires a pneumatic tourniquet. The patient has fragile skin, and equipment function and inflation time need attention.
cases.CASE12: A severely injured patient is treated in the OR, with possible medicolegal evidence. The team plans preservation and, if death occurs, appropriate handling.
cases.CASE13: A pandemic surge affects an urgent surgical service. Patient routing, personnel communication, and protective-equipment supply are under review.
cases.CASE14: An OR is reviewing equipment reliability after a recall and an intraoperative malfunction. Maintenance and a safe replacement are discussed.
cases.CASE15: A reprocessing team sorts different patient-care devices by Spaulding infection-risk class and prepares them for the appropriate validated process.

foundation.title: Professional foundations
foundation.text: Perioperative nursing integrates patient advocacy, clinical judgment, collaboration, and accountability across preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative care. A nurse practises within their role and demonstrated competence. In guideline language, shall is required, should is recommended, and may describes an option.

roles.title: Roles and competence
roles.text: Managers coordinate safe systems and resources; educators plan and evaluate learning; advanced and enhanced practice roles have defined preparation and authorization. A course or years of service alone do not prove independent competence.

routine.title: Routine and additional precautions
routine.text: Routine practices apply to every patient. A point-of-care risk assessment considers likely contact with blood, body fluids, mucosa, nonintact skin, or respiratory hazards. Additional precautions are added for a suspected or known transmission risk.

traffic.title: Traffic and respiratory controls
traffic.text: The surgical environment is managed through patient routing, room controls, limited traffic, and appropriate PPE. Airborne hazards may require a fitted respirator and a planned airway procedure; doors and clean-to-dirty flow help maintain the controlled environment.

attire.title: Attire and barriers
attire.text: Surgical attire, eye protection, masks or respirators, gowns, gloves, and surgical hand antisepsis each address different exposure pathways. Select the right barrier for the task and keep sterile gown and glove boundaries intact.

field.title: Aseptic technique
field.text: A sterile field is established close to use, observed continuously, and protected from contact, moisture, and movement outside its defined boundaries. Check package integrity before opening; treat a suspected breach as a safety concern.

prep.title: Skin preparation and draping
prep.text: Antiseptic choice and technique account for the patient, site, and product directions. Alcohol-containing products must dry and must not pool near an ignition source. Drapes create a fluid-resistant barrier but do not make an already contaminated area sterile.

devices.title: Device reprocessing
devices.text: Cleaning precedes disinfection or sterilization. Spaulding classification reflects tissue contact: critical devices enter sterile tissue and need sterilization; semicritical devices contact mucosa or nonintact skin and need at least high-level disinfection when suitable; noncritical devices contact intact skin. Follow the device-specific validated instructions.

sterile_supply.title: Sterilization and supply integrity
sterile_supply.text: Packaging, cycle monitoring, transport, storage, and traceability all affect whether a device is ready for sterile use. Immediate-use steam sterilization is for urgent unplanned needs and still requires validated processing; it is not an inventory workaround.

cleaning.title: Environmental cleaning
cleaning.text: Every case receives the scheduled environmental cleaning, with prompt management of visible contamination and additional measures when precautions require them. A clean-to-dirty workflow and approved product contact time help prevent cross-contamination.

preop.title: Preoperative verification
preop.text: Identify the patient with two approved identifiers, reconcile relevant history and allergies, verify consent and site marking, and use a meaningful team checklist. Resolve discrepancies before proceeding. Consent and advance directives require patient-centred review.

bundles.title: Perioperative prevention bundles
bundles.text: Temperature management, antimicrobial timing, wound class, VTE risk, and operative closure practices affect outcomes at different points. A bundle coordinates distinct measures while allowing patient-specific assessment and transparent documentation.

position.title: Transfer, positioning, and tissue protection
position.text: Safe transfer uses adequate personnel and aids. Positioning protects nerves, pressure areas, circulation, lines, and airway while allowing surgical access. Reassess after changes and communicate risks at handoff.

communication.title: Documentation and handoff
communication.text: Document observed care promptly and accurately. Standardized handoff conveys relevant events, unresolved issues, and required follow-up to the receiving team, with opportunity to clarify.

counts.title: Retained-item prevention
counts.text: Standardized counts track sponges, sharps, instruments, and other designated items. Personnel changes, emergency cases, intentional packing, and discrepancies require explicit communication and documentation. A correct count does not overrule a credible concern about a missing item.

specific.title: Specific care management
specific.text: Tourniquet, wound, medication, solution, and specimen handling each require checks tied to the patient and procedure. Label items clearly, reconcile time and pressure when relevant, and verify the intended specimen processing with pathology.

anesthesia.title: Anesthesia and sedation
anesthesia.text: General, regional, local, moderate sedation, and monitored anesthesia care each have different effects and preparation needs. The team plans monitoring, airway and resuscitation support, patient positioning, and safe transition to the next phase of care.

technology.title: Technology, energy, and plume
technology.text: MIS and robotic surgery require device checks and practiced emergency access. Surgical energy can cause burns or fire; coordinate oxygen, fuel, and ignition controls. Laser eyewear is hazard-specific, and surgical plume is captured near its source.

environment.title: OR environmental safety
environment.text: Lighting, noise, ventilation, temperature, humidity, electrical systems, and construction can affect patient and staff safety. Deviations are escalated through the local contingency process rather than ignored during a case.

team.title: Team and occupational safety
team.text: Credentialing, continuing education, learner supervision, and visitor controls define safe roles. Occupational risk includes biological, chemical, physical, and psychological hazards; reporting and engineering controls support safer work.

equipment.title: Equipment life cycle
equipment.text: Procurement considers clinical need, reprocessing, training, supplies, and support. Accessible instructions, preventive maintenance, recall tracking, and a malfunction response keep devices usable and traceable.

incidents.title: Incident management and disclosure
incidents.text: Near misses are intercepted before reaching a patient; no-harm incidents reach the patient without discernible harm; harmful incidents cause harm. Immediate patient care, factual documentation, reporting, review, and compassionate disclosure are coordinated through policy.

blood.title: Blood and donation
blood.text: Transfusion requires consent or documented refusal, accurate patient-product verification, monitoring, and a reaction plan. Death and donation require dignity, notification, legal considerations, and coordination with designated programs.

evidence.title: Medicolegal evidence
evidence.text: Potential evidence is identified, preserved, sealed, documented, and handed over through an approved chain of custody. Clinical care remains the priority while item identity and handling are protected.

emergency.title: Life-threatening emergencies
emergency.text: DIC, malignant hyperthermia, and cardiac arrest require early recognition, prompt communication, ready equipment, and rehearsed team roles. MH risk may be signalled by family history; rising carbon dioxide can precede fever.

pandemic.title: Pandemic response
pandemic.text: A command structure coordinates triage, patient pathways, staffing, supply, surgical priority, and education. Suspected cases are routed with precautions while status is unresolved; policies adapt as conditions change.
